extracted.intended_audience: general readers, law students, and practitioners seeking an overview of defamation law across jurisdictions
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative, jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction summary of legal standards, elements, defenses, and penalties governing defamation (civil and criminal). Useful for understanding how different systems define and assess defamatory conduct and available defences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of harm for individuals; corporate pecuniary-loss requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: As the law assumes that an individual suffers loss if a statement is defamatory, there is no need to prove that specific damage or loss has occurred. However, Section 6 of the Act allows for a defamation action brought by a corporate body to proceed only when the body corporate alleges and proves that the publication of the defamation has caused or is likely to cause pecuniary loss to that body corporate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals: harm is presumed upon showing a statement is defamatory; corporations: in some statutes/jurisdictions the plaintiff-corporation must plead and prove likely pecuniary loss (or serious financial loss).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamatory meaning standard (ordinary members of the public test)
rubrics_metrics.description: In common law provinces and territories, defamation covers any communication that tends to lower the esteem of the subject in the minds of ordinary members of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment is objective — would ordinary members of the public regard the communication as lowering the subject's reputation or esteem?

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent not required; intent presumed
rubrics_metrics.description: Intent is always presumed, and it is not necessary to prove that the defendant intended to defame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defamation actions typically do not require proof of malicious intent unless a particular defence or higher standard (e.g., actual malice for public officials in US law) is invoked by the jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences available: justification (truth), fair comment/honest opinion, responsible communication, privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a claim has been made, the defendant may avail themselves of a defence of justification (the truth), fair comment (honest opinion), responsible communication, or privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope and availability of each defence vary by jurisdiction and statutory law; some jurisdictions expand or limit these defences by statutory reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innocent dissemination defence for publishers/intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers of defamatory comments may also use the defence of innocent dissemination where they had no knowledge of the nature of the statement, it was not brought to their attention, and they were not negligent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical application: distributors, newsstands, ISPs and other intermediaries who did not know and were not negligent; statutory formulations differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate-plaintiff eligibility and special requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Common law jurisdictions vary as to whether they permit corporate plaintiffs in defamation actions. Under contemporary Australian law, private corporations are denied the right to sue for defamation, with an exception for small businesses (corporations with less than 10 employees and no subsidiaries). By contrast, Canadian law grants private corporations substantially the same right to sue for defamation as individuals. Since 2013, English law allows private corporations to sue for defamation but requires them to prove that the defamation caused both serious harm and serious financial loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether corporations can sue and, if so, what additional thresholds (serious harm, financial loss, small-business exceptions) apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actio iniuriarum elements (Roman-Dutch and related systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: For liability under the actio iniuriarum the general elements of delict must be present, but specific rules have been developed: harm (violation of a personality interest — corpus, dignitas, fama), wrongful conduct, and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harm under actio iniuriarum covers infringement of corpus (physical integrity), dignitas (dignity/self-respect — must be serious; requires contumelia) and fama (reputation). Causation is often presumed; specific regional rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contumelia requirement and deliberate affront in Scots/actio iniuriarum law
rubrics_metrics.description: The actio iniuriarum requires that the conduct of the defender be 'contumelious'—it must show such hubristic disregard of the pursuer's recognized personality interest that an intention to affront (animus iniuriandi) might be imputed. Scots law gives reparation where a non-patrimonial interest has been deliberately affronted; negligent interference is insufficient to generate liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-patrimonial (dignitary) interests require deliberate affront; mere negligence in injuring dignity normally will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal defamation definitions and penalties (general/Canada example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jurisdictions treat defamation as a criminal offence. Canadian Criminal Code defines defamatory libel as 'matter published, without lawful justification or excuse, that is likely to injure the reputation of any person by exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule.' A 'libel known to be false' can be an indictable offence with a prison term up to five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminalization varies widely; when criminal, statutes typically define an offence as publication likely to injure reputation and prescribe fines or custodial sentences. Procedural protections and frequency of use vary by country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group libel and requirement for specificity or implication of common wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: Historic common law cases show that a publication 'inveighing against mankind in general, or against a particular order of men' was not libel, but if the publication implied that a group (e.g., 'Jews') frequently committed an act, the whole community could be held to have been defamed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group libel may be actionable if the publication imputes wrongful conduct to the group as a whole or to a sufficiently identifiable subgroup; courts differ on thresholds for identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian 2006 reforms (elements, abolishing libel/slander distinction, triviality, truth defence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2006 uniform defamation laws in Australia abolished the distinction between libel and slander; provided a new defence of triviality (defendant proves plaintiff unlikely to sustain harm); greatly restricted corporations' right to sue; established truth as an unqualified defence (defendant must prove imputations are substantially true); and allowed defences to be negated by proof the publication was actuated by malice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Blue summarized the tort's ingredients: (1) defendant participates in publication to a third party; (2) the body of work contains a passage alleged to be defamatory; (3) the passage conveys an imputation; (4) the imputation is about the plaintiff; (5) the imputation is damaging to the plaintiff's reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online publication and territorial jurisdiction (Dow Jones v Gutnick example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet-published foreign publications that defamed an Australian in their Australian reputation could be held accountable under Australian defamation law (Dow Jones v Gutnick). Short communications (e.g., tweets of even three words) have been held potentially defamatory (Hockey v Fairfax / Mickle v Farley).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online and social-media publications raise jurisdictional and liability questions; short or terse statements can still meet the defamatory threshold depending on context and jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: France: truth defence limitations and 'good faith' exception criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Under French law the only statutory defence available is to demonstrate the truth of the defamatory statement, except in cases involving an individual's personal life. French courts recognize three exceptions: references to matters over ten years old; references to pardoned or expunged criminal records; and a plea of good faith which may be made if the statement pursues a legitimate aim, is not driven by animosity or malice, is prudent and measured in presentation, and is backed by a serious investigation that dutifully sought to ascertain the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In France truth may not be a defence when the matter concerns private life; the 'good faith' exception has multiple factual requirements focusing on legitimate aim and reasonable investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: China (civil): personality-rights framework and verification considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: China's Civil Code recognizes personality rights (reputation, honour, privacy, dignity); liability covers fact fabrication, distortion, lack of verification, and misrepresentation. Verification considerations include source credibility, controversial information, timeliness, public order and morals. Rights to request correction or deletion and remedies for infringement are specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chinese law foregrounds duties of verification and provides statutory remediation routes (correction/deletion); criminal provisions (e.g., Article 246) may punish serious defamation with imprisonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quebec civil standard: injury, wrongful act, causation, and reasonableness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish civil liability for defamation in Quebec the plaintiff must establish, on a balance of probabilities, the existence of an injury (fault), a wrongful act (damage), and a causal connection. Defamation in Quebec is governed by a reasonableness standard (as opposed to strict liability); a defendant who made a false statement would not be held liable if it was reasonable to believe the statement was true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quebec applies civil-code reasonableness concepts rather than common-law strict presumptions of harm; the defendant's belief/reasonableness at the time is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: India: criminal defamation definition, exceptions, time limit and procedural character
rubrics_metrics.description: In India, a defamation case can be filed under criminal or civil law. Criminal defamation (formerly Section 499 of the IPC, replaced by Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) defines defamation as making or publishing any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm the reputation of such person. There are ten valid exceptions when a statement is not considered defamation. Punishment may be simple imprisonment for up to two years, or a fine, or both. Criminal defamation is prosecuted only upon a complaint (within six months) and is bailable, non-cognisable and compoundable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural limits (complaint requirement, limitation period) and statutory exceptions are important; defamation can be both civil and criminal in India.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republication/hyperlink liability (Canadian Supreme Court example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court of Canada held that a person who posts hyperlinks on a website which lead to another site with defamatory content is not publishing that defamatory material for the purposes of libel and defamation law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability for republication, linking, or aggregation of content is treated differently across jurisdictions; hyperlinking may not amount to publication in some courts, but facts and context matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors and higher penalties for public dissemination or protected classes/officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Many statutes increase penalties or treat offences more severely where defamation occurs in public, damages multiple people, targets public officials, or involves protected characteristics; e.g., Belgium doubles minimum penalties when motivated by hatred toward protected characteristics; some countries impose higher penalties for defaming authorities or public servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or advising on defamation risk, identify aggravating factors (publicity, targeting officials or protected groups, incitement to violence) that elevate penalties or likelihood of criminal prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual exemptions for certain expression types (scientific, literary, journalistic, artistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions exempt statements made in scientific works, literary works, works of art, public information by politicians, journalistic work, or in defence of rights where conduct was not aimed at damaging reputation (e.g., Croatia's criminal code context-based exemptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context (purpose, medium, audience) can determine whether allegedly defamatory material is actionable; many codes carve out protections for bona fide public-interest or cultural expression.
